---
title: "Native vs LightGBM benchmark"
---

Medium-scale holdout comparison of the built-in histogram trainer (`backend = 'native'`) against in-process LightGBM (`backend = 'lightgbm'`) on a deterministic synthetic tabular problem. Numbers come from the committed results file produced by [`scripts/native_benchmark/run.py`](https://github.com/JavOrraca/duckboost/blob/main/scripts/native_benchmark/run.py).

::: {.callout-important}
## How to read this
Same hyperparameter MAP for both backends, ~200k rows, ~20% hash holdout. This is evidence that the native path learns useful structure at a moderate scale — not a bake-off that LightGBM loses in general. LightGBM still wins on huge data, GPU, and vendor-only features.
:::

**Generated:** `2026-10-01T08:09:33.147409+00:00`  
**Rows:** 200,000 (seed `7`)  
**Host:** `Linux-6.12.94+-x86_64-with-glibc2.39`

**Shared train options**

| Option | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `n_estimators` | `80` |
| `max_depth` | `5` |
| `learning_rate` | `0.1` |
| `min_samples_leaf` | `20` |
| `max_bins` | `64` |
| `reg_lambda` | `1.0` |
| `subsample` | `0.8` |
| `colsample_bytree` | `0.8` |
| `seed` | `7` |

Both runs also set `categorical_features` to `cat_a,cat_b,cat_c,cat_d`.

## Holdout results

| Task | Backend | Metric | Holdout | Secondary | Train seconds |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| regression | `native` | rmse | 0.238832 |  | 10.650 |
| regression | `lightgbm` | rmse | 0.244557 |  | 16.337 |
| binary | `native` | logloss | 0.048162 | accuracy=0.9937 | 8.343 |
| binary | `lightgbm` | logloss | 0.057630 | accuracy=0.9921 | 20.416 |

## Takeaways from this run

- **Regression RMSE:** native `0.2388` vs LightGBM `0.2446` (train `10.7` s vs `16.3` s).
- **Binary logloss:** native `0.0482` vs LightGBM `0.0576` (accuracy `0.9937` vs `0.9921`; train `8.3` s vs `20.4` s).


## Problem design

Synthetic rows from `range(n)`:

| Feature group | Columns | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Categorical | `cat_a`…`cat_d` | Low-cardinality integer codes (`% 17`, `% 9`, …) |
| Continuous | `x1`…`x8` | Sines/cosines, scaled remainders, logs |
| Regression target | `y_reg` | Additive signal + `sin × cat` interaction + small noise |
| Binary target | `y_bin` | Threshold on a related score |
| Split | `split` | `hash(i, seed) % 5 = 0` → `test`, else `train` |

Train wall time is measured with `epoch_ms(current_timestamp)` immediately before and after the `duckboost_train` aggregate (dataset build excluded). Holdout metrics use `duckboost_evaluate_agg` on the test split only.

## Reproduce

```bash
# LightGBM-linked release build
EXT_FLAGS='-DDUCKBOOST_WITH_LIGHTGBM=ON' make release

python3 scripts/native_benchmark/run.py --n-rows 200000 --seed 7
# refreshes scripts/native_benchmark/results.json — re-render this page to update the table
```

See [`scripts/native_benchmark/README.md`](https://github.com/JavOrraca/duckboost/blob/main/scripts/native_benchmark/README.md) for flags and caveats.

## What this does *not* show

- Public leaderboard datasets (Higgs, airline, …)
- Multi-million-row throughput or multithreaded native training
- Vendor-only knobs (monotonic constraints, GPU, GOSS/EFB)
- Perfect hyperparameter parity — DuckDB maps a shared MAP into each backend

For the SQL walkthrough on real CSVs, see the [native trainer vignette](vignettes/native-trainer.qmd).
